body: Serbian bollards are often flat and have an off-centered reflector.
Serbia exclusively uses B-Profile guardrails, which helps distinguish it from North Macedonia.
Serbia uses chevrons with a black arrow on a white background, a design also found in Slovenia, Montenegro, and North Macedonia.
Serbian licence plates are white with a blue strip, while agricultural vehicles have distinctive green plates.
The Serbian language uses both Cyrillic and Latin scripts. The Cyrillic letters Ђ, ђ, Ћ, and ћ are unique to Serbian.
When written in the Latin script, Serbian uses special letters like Č, Ć, Đ, Š, and Ž, which are also found in Croatian and Montenegrin.
Most Google Street View coverage in Serbia was captured with a car that has no antenna, a feature shared only with North Macedonia in the region.
Most of Serbia's Street View coverage is concentrated in the north (Vojvodina), around the capital Belgrade, and in the southeast near Niš. Note that Kosovo has no coverage.
Northern Serbia (Vojvodina) is extremely flat, while the central-southern region is hilly. The most mountainous areas are in the southwest and southeast.
Serbian area codes can help with regional identification: codes starting with 2 are in the north, 1 in the central and eastern regions, and 3 in the southwest.
The Vojvodina region in northern Serbia is a completely flat, agricultural landscape with no hills.
A slight ridge in an otherwise flat landscape is a key feature of Fruška Gora National Park, located southwest of Novi Sad.
Central-northern Serbia is characterized by slight rolling hills.
The southern Morava River basin has a rolling landscape, but with larger hills and mountains visible in the distance.
A lush, green, mountainous landscape is characteristic of southern and southeastern Serbia, along the Bulgarian and Kosovo borders.
Fall coverage can be found in the region south of Čačak and in a small area around Valjevo.
Serbia has three main divided highways visible on Street View: the A1 (E-75), A3 (E-70), and A4. Be aware that some sections shown as divided on maps may not be on Street View due to older coverage.
A white Google car with a short antenna may be visible in major cities like Novi Sad, Belgrade, and Niš, as well as on the E75 highway connecting them.
The distinct Vršac Mountains protrude from a flat landscape near the Romanian border. The area is also known for vineyards to the south and the Vršac Castle on the mountain.
Bilingual signs with both Serbian and Hungarian can be found in northern Vojvodina, where there is a significant Hungarian population.
A distinctive tadpole-shaped smudge appears on the camera in the area east of Belgrade, extending to the Romanian border.
A small section of the E-80 highway north of Pirot has unique yellow center lines.
